newsitem.title: CHINA: China and Russia boost trade with energy deals.
newsitem.headline: China and Russia boost trade with energy deals.

text.p: Visiting Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Chinese counterpart Li Peng on Friday took a giant step to boost Sino-Russian trade ties, presiding over the signing of billions of dollars in deals.

They included a $7.0-billion framework pact to supply energy-thirsty China with natural gas from a field in Russia's Irkutsk region, and a $1.5-billion agreement to supply electricity to the Chinese northeast, Russian sources said.
A Russian embassy statement said the premiers agreed to cooperate further on hydropower and nuclear projects, boost transportation links, and enhance economic joint ventures.

Li and Chernomyrdin also signed an agreement to organise regular meetings between Chinese and Russian heads of government that was hailed by Chinese President Jiang Zemin as a boost for improving ties between the two Asian giants.
"In the next century, our two countries will enjoy better relations," the Xinhua news agency quoted Jiang as saying.

Trade between the giant neighbours was just $6.8 billion in 1996, and both sides have said they want to increase that to $20 billion by the next century. Diplomats said the natural gas deal would help to achieve that aim.
"The Russian side considers this project as of strategic importance," one Russian source said.
The field would be tapped by Rusia Petroleum that groups Russia's SIDANCO oil firm and South Korea's East Asia Gas Co Ltd, a member of the Hanbo Group.
The deal called for Sino-Russian cooperation in building a pipeline to link the field with northeastern China, one diplomat said, adding that final details had yet to be worked out.
"South Korea will join the project in the form of some kind of construction and will share some of the financial debt," one source said.
China, once a net exporter of oil, has forecast oil imports could reach 50 million tonnes a year by 2000 as rapid economic growth fuels demand for energy.
Li said the accords would strengthen ties between the Asian giants, who pledged to forge a "strategic partnership" during a series of high level official visits over the past year.

"Further expanding and deepening cooperation in trade and science will establish and develop the basis for the two countries' strategic partnership going into the 21st century," state television quoted Li as saying.
Sino-Russian ties have gradually warmed since 1989 when the two formally patched up relations after years of territorial disputes and a struggle for leadership of the communist world.
The political warming climaxed in April when presidents Jiang Zemin and Boris Yeltsin met in Moscow and outlined their visions of the post-Cold War order.

Among other deals signed on Friday was a railroad agreement that seeks to increase Sino-Russian rail freight by allowing Russian railcars to run directly on Chinese rails, a feat now impossible because of different rail gauges in the two nations.
Chinese and Russian businessmen also signed deals for two joint ventures, including one to make Russian-designed trucks in northern China, the Russian embassy statement said.

Another pact called for the creation of a technology and science development zone in Russia. The two premiers had also agreed that Russia's Hong Kong consulate would continue in the territory after it returns to China on July 1, it said.
Chernomyrdin's three-day visit is scheduled to end on Saturday.
